title: TA9-08466
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXXXX and his spouse, XXXXXXXXX and their two minor chidren, XXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXX, all citizens of Czech Republic, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 The claimants' identities have been established through certified copies of the claimants' passports.2
XXXXXXXXX was appointed as the Designated Representative for her two minor children pursuant to section 167(2) of the IRPA.

The claimant alleges that as a Roma in the Czech Republic he was discriminated against and assaulted because of his skin colour and ethnicity as Roma. He made the following allegations in the Personal Information Form (PIF):3
In XXX 2006, the claimant and his spouse were physically assaulted by a couple of white Czechs, causing the claimant injuries to his arm and hand.

In XXX 2007, the claimant and his spouse were stopped on the road and assaulted by two white men. The next day the female claimant was visited at her work and threatened not to report the incident to the police.
One time at a pub, the claimant was stabbed simply because he is a gypsy.
The female claimant, when she was pregnant, was given some pills to take.
The claimants left the Czech Republic on XXXXX, 2009 and arrived in Canada and made a claim for refugee protection on the same date.

At a hearing on October 25, 2011, the claimants testified that the information contained in the PIF had not been translated to them, so the hearing was adjourned to allow them the opportunity to review and amend their PIF as necessary.
On December 5, 2011, the claimant submitted an amended narrative to his PIF.4 In this narrative the claimant made the following allegations:

In XXXXXX 2004, the female claimant was attacked while in a restaurant causing her to require surgery. The claimants allege that they were attacked in XXXXX 2005, XXX 2006, XXX 2007, XXXXXX 2008 and XXXXXX 2008.

At the hearing on January 3, 2012, the claimant testified that the information contained in the original narrative to the PIF was inaccurate and thus was relying on the information contained in the amended narrative.

I find that the claimant has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground, or that he would personally be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to his country. Therefore, I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. As the claim of his wife and his minor children rely entirely on the evidence of the claimant, their claims must also fail.

The determinative issue in this case is whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In this regard, I considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in the Czech Republic, whether the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. State Protection

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. Having canvassed the country conditions documents, I find that Czech Republic is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country.5

To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" confirmation of the state's inability to protect its citizens.6 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board, that the evidence establishes that the state protection is in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.7 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.8 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.9 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.10

Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection, to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.11 To qualify for refugee status, a claimant must satisfy the Board that he or she sought, but was unable to obtain, protection from their home state, or alternatively, that their home state, on an objective basis, could not be expected to provide protection.12 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.13

A claimant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.14 In a functioning democracy, a claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.15 The documentary evidence16 before the Board indicates that Czech Republic is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Therefore, in countries such as Czech Republic, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.17 Local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.18

The Board is not obliged to prove that the Czech Republic can offer the applicant effective state protection, rather, the applicant bears the legal burden of rebutting the presumption that adequate state protection exists by adducing clear and convincing evidence which satisfies the Board on a balance of probabilities.19

I find that the claimant has not provided clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in the Czech Republic is inadequate. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.20 I considered whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps in his circumstances to seek protection.

The claimant was questioned as to what efforts he made to seek state protection before fleeing the Czech Republic. The claimant testified that in XXXXXX 2004 and in XXX 2006, he was verbally attacked and in an attempt to defend him, his common law spouse was assaulted and sustained injuries for which she required medical attention. The claimant testified that they reported the incidents to the police and in doing so was able to identify the perpetrators to them only by saying that that the person was heavier, bald and white and that in one incident, one of the men was tall. The claimant testified that they reported the incidents to the police each time in hopes that they would apprehend the perpetrators, but although the police made a written report each time and told them that they would investigate, nothing happened. The claimant was asked how he expected the police to apprehend the perpetrators, with only the general description he had given them of the perpetrators, and he testified that he had expected the police to speak to witnesses in order to make the arrests. The claimant testified that the police did not give him a copy of the reports because they told him that the investigation was not finished and the claimant testified that he did not check back with the police to inquire as to the status of the investigation at any time. I find that by the police making written reports of the incidents and stating that they would investigate the incidents is evidence of the state showing a willingness to offer protection to its citizens. Given the vague and general descriptions given of the perpetrators, the fact that no one may have been apprehended is not clear and convincing evidence that the state is unable to provide its citizens with adequate protection. No state is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times and the fact that the state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens. 21 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.22 In the absence of a detailed description of the perpetrators, I find the claimant has failed to provide the police with information which may have been necessary to assist them in properly identifying and apprehending the perpetrators, and as such, I find the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection.

The claimant testified that in XXXXX 2005, he was attacked and injured, and reported the incident to the police, but because he was unable to identify the perpetrator he was told that they could not investigate. I find that there is insufficient evidence to indicate that the protection being offered to the claimant in this situation was inadequate. Given the circumstances, I find that the claimant's expectation that the police should have been able to find and apprehend the perpetrators, even though the claimant himself was unable to identify them in any way, is not reasonable. Again I find that the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of adequate state protection with clear and convincing evidence.

The claimant testified that in XXXXXX 2008, he suffered serious injuries as a result of an attack which occurred in a restaurant, whereby he was stabbed in his leg and a cut in his neck by the owner/waiter of the restaurant. The claimant testified that although the hospital reported the incident to the police and the police contacted the claimant, went to his house and took a written report, nothing happened. The claimant testified that the police told him that they would investigate and let him know when they got more information but he was never contacted. The claimant testified that although he had expected the police to attend the restaurant and speak to witnesses and ultimately apprehend the perpetrator, nothing was done. The claimant testified that the alleged perpetrator disappeared and nothing happened. The claimant testified that as he never heard back from the police, approximately one month later and again a week after that, he attended the police station to inquire as to the status of the investigation and the police told him that they were continuing to examine the incident and that they were working on it. The claimant testified that he was never given a copy of any of the police reports made and that when he requested them he was told each time that as it was not completed they would not give him a copy. I find there is insufficient evidence to indicate that adequate protection was not provided to the claimant. Each time the claimant approached the police with information pertaining to the incident, they made a report and initiated an investigation. No evidence was adduced to indicate that the claimant sought any state assistance beyond that of the police. I find there is insufficient evidence to indicate that the protection being offered by the state was inadequate. Although the claimant testified that no witnesses had been contacted by the police, insufficient reliable and probative evidence was provided to substantiate that assertion. Based on the evidence adduced, I find that the police took action based on the information they had been provided to protect the claimant.

The Board finds that it would be unreasonable to expect in any society that all violent acts reported to police would result in immediate prosecutions or convictions. The Federal Court has held that a claimant's decision to flee before police have had an opportunity to properly respond to and investigate a transgression did not amount to a lack of state protection.23 In this particular case, there is no information to suggest that police were not making genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimant's allegations and apprehend the claimant's perpetrator.

I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation to indicate that there is widespread reporting of incidents of intolerance, discrimination and persecution of Romani individuals in the Czech Republic. However, weighted against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that the Czech Republic candidly acknowledges its past problems, and is making serious efforts to rectify the treatment of minorities in that country, especially in the case of the Roma. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is an adequate state protection in the Czech Republic for Roma who are victims of crime, police abuse, discrimination or persecution, that the Czech Republic is making serious efforts to address these problems, and that the police and government officials are both willing and able to protect victims.

There is documentary evidence that indicates Roma are discriminated against. The documents indicate that although violent attacks on foreigners and the Roma minority had declined since the 1990s, remaining largely out of the headlines,24 societal prejudice against the country's Romani population occasionally manifested itself in violence.25

The documentary evidence indicates that the state does not condone or acquiesce to this racial and discriminatory behavior, particularly at the hands of extremist skinheads. For example, in the mid-1990s, the Ministry of the Interior launched an initiative to combat extremism, allowing for police monitoring of extremist group activities and trends.26

The documentary evidence indicates the police in the Czech Republic respond to incidents where Roma have been attacked. For instance, on December 10, 2010, a regional court sentenced a youth to a three-year suspended sentence for attempted reckless endangerment, and his mother to an 18-month suspended sentence for not stopping her son from throwing a Molotov cocktail into a bedroom of the Romani home where a 14-year-old girl was the target. In another example, on October 20, 2010, a court found four men guilty of attempted murder and property damage after they were convicted of throwing Molotov cocktails into the home of a Romani family. The judge found the crime to involve extraordinary circumstances that allowed for more stringent sentencing, in the range of 20 to 22 years. These are the longest sentences ever handed down for a racially motivated crime. Relating to another incident, the Prime Minister and other government officials released statements condemning a mayor's actions who posted a statement on the city's official website declaring a "war on gypsies." Police arrested a number of right wing extremists during 2009, including 24 individuals, 18 of whom were charged with supporting and promoting movement aimed at suppressing the rights and freedoms of the individual. It was determined that a member of the Czech military was responsible for training these individuals, and he was subsequently discharged from the military without severance pay or pension. In 2008, estimated 1000 police officers used force to prevent an estimated 500 well-earned, right wing rioters from attacking Roma. The only people charged in this incident, were two Roma, who were sentenced to community service for physically and verbally assaulting members of the Workers Party. However, as a direct result of this incident, the government increased police presence in Romani neighborhoods. There are numerous other examples in the documentary evidence to demonstrate the Czech Republic's willingness and ability to protect its Romani citizens.27

In May 2008, police successfully prevented a major clash between anarchists and neo-Nazis in Brno, expelling the latter from the city. At the November 2008 Workers' Party march in Litvinov, police were able to break up the demonstrations. In December 2008, the police prevented the far-right National Party from holding demonstrations in Brno.28 At several of these demonstrations, police put their own lives at risk protecting Czech citizens, including the Roma. These efforts clearly indicate that the state is able to offer adequate protection to the Roma.

The documentary evidence notes that "the judicial proceedings on racial crime have increased in recent years due to the efforts of NGO's."29 The Czech Ombudsman was created in 1999, and is known as the Public Defender of Rights. The Ombudsman investigates allegations of public sector mistreatment of Roma and may take corrective action or issue advice or recommendations. The Ombudsman has successfully intervened in areas such as housing, but has yet to receive any formal complaints against the police.30 There are other government and non government agencies available to assist the Roma, including 400 Roma NGO's, the Czech Trade Inspectorate (to deal with unfair business practices or consumer discrimination), and the Social Inclusion Agency to address the social integration of the Roma into Czech society, including housing, health care, employment, social services and cohesion.31

There are legitimate concerns from some groups that there is impunity for racially motivated attacks and, the police responses are not sufficient; however, the preponderance of evidence indicates that the state is taking action against extremists and does not condone or assent to extremist actions.

The documents indicate the Roma faced a higher levels of poverty, unemployment, and literacy, as well as, varying levels of discrimination in education, employment, and housing.32 A 2006 Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs study found that more than 330 "excluded" localities or ghettos in the country were almost exclusively inhabited by Roma.33 Discrimination against the Roma is prevalent, but there is evidence that the Czech Republic is taking steps to assist the Roma in several ways to ensure they will be able to participate in the Czech society. For example, in January 2008 the Czech government established an agency for the social inclusion of Romani communities whose aim is to combat social exclusion, the formation of ghettos and improve the socio-economic conditions of Roma through improved access to employment and mainstream education.34 The Inter-ministerial Commission for Romani Community Affairs continued to take an active role in resolving disputes between Romani communities and their non-Romani neighbours, and promoted anti-discrimination initiatives in housing and education. The Agency for Social Inclusion in Roma Localities now operates in 15 communities. Police set up an information campaign to recruit minorities into the police force in Prague, Usti and Labem and Brno.35 Roma children continued to suffer discrimination and segregation at school despite policies for inclusion. However, the government continued steps to address discrimination in the education of Romani children during the year. In 2009, the Ministry of Education created a new Department for Equal Opportunities in Education, and in March 2010, approved the Plan for Inclusive Education to address these problems. However, in October the new minister of education halted all work on the plan. Two employees of the ministry charged with implementing changes to "practical" schools resigned due to reservations over the new direction taken by the ministry. The minister of education stated that he would present new decrees for the inclusion of Romani students in February 2011.36 The government has made efforts to encourage Roma children to pursue education. The government is encouraging Roma parents to send their children to nursery school for 3 years; it is subsidizing kindergarten; it is recruiting Roma teaching assistants for regular schools, and it is providing support programs for Roma high school students.37

The Agency for Social Inclusion in the Roma Localities continued its efforts in implementing a long-term integration plan for the Roma. The agency synchronizes and evaluates social integration efforts by ministries and municipalities. In one successful program, The Ministry of the Interior, the local government, the police force, and NGOs collaborated to provide improved housing, trained Romani mentors to ensure that Romani offenders complete probation to avoid incarceration, higher police assistance to prevent crime, provide inclusion training to teachers, offer debt education training two young girls, and ensure media coverage of successful Roma. This program was expanded to seven additional areas and encompassed 28 ongoing projects.38

Relating to national minorities and internal security, falling under a number of activities undertaken by the Czech Republic Police under its strategy of work with national minorities: * continuing activities of minority liaison officers and their working groups at Regional Headquarters of the Czech Republic Police, * the broadening of any project of Czech Republic Police Assistance working in socially excluded locations, to provide support to crime victims in socially excluded locations into more efficiently detect latent crime in such locations, * the Czech Republic Police City Headquarters in Brno completed a one-year pilot project testing the uses of supervision as a personal management tool in the Czech Republic Police, * the work on surveys mapping crime in socially excluded locations continued.39

Despite these efforts by the Czech government, statistics indicate that Roma are still underemployed and less educated. Critics claim these programs do not go far enough or are just superficial. Even so, the preponderance of evidence is that there are programs in place and the government has taken serious efforts to improve the lives of the Romani minority. However, not all of the documentary evidence currently before the Board is negative, and indicates that the Czech Republic is attempting to correct its historical discrimination against the Roma people. In particular, Board documents indicate police recruiting programs aimed at recruiting from within the Roma communities have taken place in both 2003 and 2007.40 In addition to this, as many as 130 police specialists in the Czech Republic now deal specifically with issues of "extremism, racism and other manifestations of xenophobia."41 The latest report available to the Board indicates that the police in the Czech Republic now employ Roma Police Assistants and Minority Liaison Officers to help bridge the gap between the police and the Roma communities, and several police stations report employing Romani police officers.

The documentary evidence indicates that there are numerous recourses available to Roma victims when police refuse to respond or respond inadequately to requests for state protection, and describes procedures for filing a complaint against the police, such as making a report to The Inspection of the Police of the Czech Republic, an independent body under the Minister of the Interior; or citizens can also register "complaints about police inaction and non-serious offenses by police officers" with the Office of Internal Control, which is part of the Police of the Czech Republic; or to the Office of Internal Inspection; or to the Ombudsman.42

Also of note in this instance, is that the Czech Republic is not an island unto its own, but it is a responsible member of the European Union and reports regularly to the governance structures within that Union. Even if criticism of the Czech Republic's measures to combat racism is warranted, particularly against the Romani population, on a balance of probabilities, The Czech Republic is taking the measures to implement the standards that are mandated as a member of the European Union. In the Third Report43 regarding protection of national minorities in the Czech Republic, the government reports measures taken to improve the implementation of the framework convention, such as: the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages; culture: code of administrative procedure; act on equal treatment and protection against discrimination (Anti-discrimination Act); Agency for Social Inclusion in Roma locations; education of Roma Children and efforts relating to the participation of persons belonging to national minorities and public affairs. According to the Report comprehensive annual monitoring and assessment reports on the situation of national minorities in the Czech Republic, considered and adopted by the Government, having published since 2001. Relating to activities promoting the integration of socially excluded polluted Roma population, the Report, indicates that the Czech government has benefited from the European Union structural funds for the 2007-2013 programming cycle in order to establish and staff an institution providing support to programs and projects designed to bring about radical improvement of the social and economic conditions of the Roma, including their standard of living and their access to the job market and mainstream education. Furthermore, the situation in the Czech Republic concerning extremism remains comparable with that of other EU member states.44

Counsel submitted that despite the claimant approaching the police for protection relating to numerous incidents, the police failed to take any concrete steps to provide the claimant's with protection. Counsel submitted that despite the availability of witnesses there is no evidence that the police took any action to apprehend the perpetrators and that this inaction of the police is consistent with the country condition documentation45 indicating that the police are insensitive and to the needs of the Roma people and in some instances even refuse to investigate incidents of abuse. Although this may be the case for some Roma people in certain circumstances, I find there is insufficient evidence to indicate that his was the case for this particular claimant. When this claimant reported the incidents to the police a report was taken and an investigation was initiated in all instances where the claimant was able to supply them with the necessary information. I find that even if no one was apprehended in the incidents, that it is not clear and convincing evidence the police are either unwilling or unable to provide this claimant with protection.

Counsel submitted that Roma people also face overt public hostility and discrimination exists in education and that the claimant, who has two minor children would face such discrimination if returned to the Czech Republic. Although documentary evidence indicates that such discrimination exists, I find that insufficient evidence was adduced in this particular case to indicate that that would be the case for these particular claimants, or that if it did, that it would amount to the level of persecution.

Having considered the totality of the evidence, I find that the claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence, and that the claimant did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances to avail himself of that protection before making a claim for refugee protection. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of the Czech Republic would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it.

There is no persuasive evidence before me that the claimant would face persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to his life, or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, if he returned to the Czech Republic. For all these reasons, I find that that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA, as state protection is available to him.
As the claim of his wife and his minor children rely entirely on the evidence of the claimant, their claims must also fail.

Having considered all the evidence and submissions, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor is he a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 97(1)(a) and 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

Accordingly, the Refugee Protection Division rejects their claims for refugee protection.
